expectations.text: The reply has the CTO say plainly to the board that the responsibility is the CTO's (leadership's), not the team lead's.
expectations.evidence: To the board: 'Tell the board first, plainly: "This happened on my watch, and I own it."' Board line: '"I'm accountable for this outage... If it shows our process failed, then the process, and my oversight of it, changes."' The opening sets out that the failure is the system's, not the lead's: 'a failure of the system around the migration, and you own that system.'

expectations.text: The reply recommends against firing the team lead as a response to the incident, unless a review finds misconduct or recklessness, and explains why scapegoating makes systems less safe.
expectations.evidence: 'Don't fire the platform team lead now.' Why it makes things less safe: 'teaches every engineer to hide risk next time' and 'You'd lose the person who understands the system best, right when you need them for recovery.' Exception: 'If someone knowingly bypassed an agreed control, handle it through your normal HR process, proportionately and with the person heard. That is a finding, not a starting point.'

expectations.text: The reply proposes a blameless post-mortem focused on how the system and process allowed the failure (for example testing, rollback plan, change approval, staging), with dates and owners for fixes.
expectations.evidence: 'Commission a blameless post-mortem led by someone independent of the platform team: timeline, decisions and who made them, what rollback existed, which warnings were raised. Aim for two to three weeks.' Fixes: 'every action has an owner, a date and a measure, such as a timed rollback rehearsal, a named go/no-go sign-off, and no migration without a tested fallback.' It asks 'was there a rehearsed rollback, a go/no-go review, and who approved the weekend window?'

expectations.text: The reply tells the CTO what to bring the board instead: the facts of the incident, the causes, the concrete changes and how they will know it worked.
expectations.evidence: All four elements are there, though the facts and causes come through the review rather than as an itemised board paper. Facts and causes: the independent review 'reporting back in three weeks', covering 'timeline, decisions and who made them, what rollback existed, which warnings were raised'. Changes: 'every fix owned and dated'. How they will know it worked: 'every action has an owner, a date and a measure, such as a timed rollback rehearsal... Report monthly.'

expectations.text: The reply looks after the team lead and the team, for example a private conversation and protection from public blame.
expectations.evidence: Lead: 'Tell the lead yourself, before they hear it elsewhere, what the board raised and what you're doing.' Team: 'Make sure the team is rested and not left to absorb the blame.'

expectations.text: The reply opens with the recommendation and stays concise (roughly 500 words or less).
expectations.evidence: 455 words by wc -w (limit 550). Opens with the recommendation: 'Don't fire the platform team lead now. Take the accountability yourself, and give the board an independent post-mortem with owned, dated fixes.'

factual_errors.evidence: No wrong rule, number or date. The Dutch dismissal claim is general and correct.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon. 'Steelmanned' is ordinary English, not skill jargon.

owns_result.evidence: 'This happened on my watch, and I own it.' / 'I'm accountable for this outage.'

best_insight.value: It gives a ready board line that pairs the CTO's accountability with a dated review and a conditional promise ('If it shows individual misconduct, we'll act on it'), which meets the board's demand without giving in to it, in under 460 words.

suggestions.assertion: The reply looks after the team lead and the team, for example a private conversation and protection from public blame.
suggestions.reason: The examples (private conversation, protection from public blame) both concern the lead, but the text also says 'and the team'. That clause decided two samples that were strong on the lead but said nothing about the wider team that worked the 9-hour outage. Say whether wider-team care is required and what counts (rest after the incident, telling the team, keeping them out of the board's blame).

suggestions.assertion: The reply tells the CTO what to bring the board instead: the facts of the incident, the causes, the concrete changes and how they will know it worked.
suggestions.reason: 'How they will know it worked' is the element samples most often miss: they offer monthly progress reports or 'a visible gate', which show the fixes were done, not that they work. Name what counts (a timed rollback rehearsal, change failure rate, no migration without a tested fallback) or make it a separate assertion.

No assertion checks whether the leader offers a tangible consequence of their own (bonus, formal review of their own role), which answers the board's wish for visible accountability head-on and follows the 'take the first cut yourself' principle. Only one sample did this.

Assertions 2 and 3 passed for all four samples here; they guard the core of the answer but did not separate samples. Factual accuracy on Dutch dismissal law is also unchecked by any assertion, though every sample made claims about it.

eval_feedback.overall: The best sample: concise (455 words) and covers every assertion, including care for the wider team and a measure for each fix; its board deliverable is the least itemised of the passes.
